messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-four when the warehouse fire started. He had been working the night shift at the distribution center for seven years—a reliable, quiet man who showed up on time and kept to himself during breaks. On that February night, he was in the loading bay when the sprinkler system failed. A forklift operator, rushing to meet a deadline, had disabled the alarm to avoid triggering a false evacuation. When the fire broke out in the adjacent storage unit, no one was notified. Marcus smelled smoke first, then saw the orange glow creeping across the ceiling. He ran toward the back exit, but the door had been locked from the outside—a safety violation no one had flagged. For eight minutes, he was trapped in a corridor filling with black smoke, his hands pressed against the warm metal door frame, screaming. When firefighters finally cut through, his palms were blistered and his lungs scorched. Two of his coworkers didn't make it out.

The aftermath was a blur of hospital stays and investigations. Marcus returned to work after three months, telling himself and his wife, Elena, that he was fine. He wasn't. Within weeks, certain moments would ambush him—the texture of the warehouse's rough concrete wall, which he sometimes felt in his mind's hands, would send him spiraling. When he encountered a coworker behaving recklessly—cutting corners, ignoring protocol—the old rage and terror would spike together. And the proximity of other people in crowded spaces, especially in enclosed areas, made his chest tighten in ways he couldn't explain.

What frightened Marcus most was how real the memories felt. When he recalled those eight minutes, they didn't feel like something that had happened two years ago. The snapshot images—his hands burning against the metal, the smoke so thick he couldn't see his own fingers, the sound of his own screaming—were vivid and immediate in a way that normal memories never were. Ordinary moments, by contrast, felt like they were happening behind frosted glass. He would come home from work and Elena would tell him about her day, and he would realize he'd absorbed almost nothing. But the fire—every sensory detail of those eight minutes felt more real than the life he was actually living. The shame came with these memories, hot and suffocating: shame that he'd panicked, shame that he'd survived when others hadn't, shame that he couldn't seem to move past it.

Over time, Marcus developed ways to manage the intrusions. When a memory surfaced—the texture of the concrete, the heat, the screaming—he would tell himself it wasn't really that bad, that his mind was exaggerating, that the event itself had been less severe than he was remembering. He would push the thoughts away with force, clenching his teeth and turning his attention obsessively to his phone or the television. But these strategies only worked for minutes. The suppression would fracture, and the memories would return sharper and more insistent. When that happened, Marcus would sometimes pinch the inside of his forearm hard enough to leave marks, or press his fingernails into his palm until they drew blood. The physical pain was clean and simple—it interrupted the memory, gave his mind something immediate and controllable to focus on.

Yet the cycles were tightening. Encountering someone at work who bent safety rules—a young cashier who propped open a fire door to avoid walking around—would trigger the memories, and the memories would feel so vivid and real that Marcus would need to suppress them, and the suppression would fail, and he would hurt himself to regain control. The triggers were everywhere. Even the texture of certain fabrics in the stockroom—a rough synthetic blend that reminded him of the warehouse wall—would set everything in motion again. Elena had noticed the small wounds on his arms and asked about them once. He'd deflected. He couldn't explain that hurting himself was the only thing that made the memories stop, that the pain was a kind of relief. Two weeks ago, his manager had called him into the office to discuss his performance. Marcus was making mistakes, forgetting inventory counts, calling in sick more often. He'd nearly had a panic attack standing near the loading dock. He told Elena that night that he needed help, that something was very wrong and he didn't know how to fix it himself. For the first time since the fire, he was afraid not of the memories themselves, but of what his attempts to escape them were doing to him.
